desc:
A shared calendar receives booking requests one after another. A request [start, end) is a half-open range. The calendar tolerates a double booking, but never a triple one: a request is accepted if, after adding it to the accepted events, no moment is covered by three or more accepted events; otherwise it is rejected and the calendar stays unchanged.

Process the requests in the given order and return an array with 1 for every accepted request and 0 for every rejected one.

requests = [[10, 20], [50, 60], [10, 40], [5, 15], [5, 10], [25, 55]]
result   = [1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1]

[5, 15) is rejected because [10, 15) is already covered by [10, 20) and [10, 40). [5, 10) is fine since it only touches that double-booked region.
hints: Checking a request against the accepted events one pair at a time is not enough: three events can overlap even if no single pair looks dangerous. What kind of region is dangerous?
A new request is bad exactly when it overlaps a region that is already covered twice. Keep a list of such double-covered ranges.

Keep two lists: accepted events and double-covered ranges. A request is rejected if it overlaps any double range. Otherwise accept it and add its intersection with every accepted event to the double ranges (use max(starts) and min(ends) and keep the intersection only if it is non-empty).
editorial: Maintain events (all accepted ranges) and doubles (every range covered by at least two accepted events). A request [s, e) would create a triple booking if and only if it shares a moment with some range of doubles: any such moment is already covered twice, and the request adds a third cover.

If it passes that test, accept it. Its overlaps with existing events become new double-covered ranges, so append [max(s, a), min(e, b)] for every accepted event [a, b) when that range is not empty. Because the request does not touch any old double range, no moment can be covered more than twice, and the invariant holds. Each request costs O(n), so the total is O(n2) time and O(n) space, fine for 1,000 requests.
A sweep alternative: for each request, add it tentatively to the events, sort the events and check the running count; that is O(n<sup>2</sup> log n) overall.
